headings.title: SMTO-AUT-0040 — This Microsoft sign-in doesn't match an open request

html:
SMTO-AUT-0040 — This Microsoft sign-in doesn't match an open request

GUID: 6db7aa87-8c8e-599b-9187-a740ecc3407d
Slug: microsoft-oauth-state-invalid
Domain: AUT · Subsystem: microsoft

What happened

  • Microsoft sent you back to SMTO, but SMTO had no open sign-in waiting for that reply. The link may have been used already, replaced, or cleared when SMTO restarted. No Microsoft account was connected or changed.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Close the old Microsoft sign-in tab, then ask SMTO in a conversation to connect your Microsoft 365 account again so you get a new link. Each sign-in link works only once, so an old, bookmarked or reloaded page is refused.
  2. Open the new link in the same browser and finish Microsoft's pages within ten minutes. Don't restart SMTO or edit the Microsoft OAuth App entry in Parameter Store meanwhile. SMTO keeps the open sign-in only while it is running and checks that the app settings haven't changed.
  3. If you open SMTO through a different web address than usual, such as a company proxy address, tell the person who manages SMTO. SMTO refuses replies that come back to a different address than the one Microsoft was told to use.

What success looks like

  • The browser shows a page that starts with Connected and says you can close the window.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them, with the time you tried, to the person who manages SMTO's Microsoft 365 setup. Don't keep reloading the old sign-in page; it will never work again.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • The shared browser authorization flow rejected a Microsoft 365 callback or launch ticket: no matching pending state (already used, superseded, expired ticket or lost on Server restart), duplicate code/state/error parameters, a callback URL different from the pending redirect_uri, or a changed Microsoft OAuth App revision.

What this means

  • The Microsoft callback contains duplicate fields or fails the shared flow's pending-state, lifetime, callback or application-revision checks. Authorization establishes a particular connection, account and scope. It neither expands operation permissions nor proves the outcome of a request already dispatched.

Why this can happen

  • The Microsoft callback contains duplicate fields or fails the shared flow's pending-state, lifetime, callback or application-revision checks.

How to diagnose it

  • Start from the current Settings connection request and compare its registered callback and application revision.

How to fix it

  • Start a new microsoft365.connect (or POST /api/agent/microsoft365/auth/start) and complete it once, in one browser, against the same Server process within 600 seconds. For confidential clients, make sure the externally reconstructed callback URL exactly equals the registered redirect_uri (reverse-proxy scheme, host and port), and do not edit the microsoft_oauth_app record while consent is pending; expiry detected at callback time is reported separately as oauth_timeout.
  • Start a new Microsoft connection from Settings and complete that request in the same browser session.

Retry and execution caution

  • Confirm current state and correct the reported condition before requesting another attempt. Do not replay work with an unknown outcome.

How to verify the fix

  • A fresh single-use Microsoft callback matches the current pending sign-in and registered application.

What not to do

  • Do not delete retained evidence or retry an operation whose effect is unknown.

Technical notes

  • Authorization establishes a particular connection, account and scope. It neither expands operation permissions nor proves the outcome of a request already dispatched.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
